front.title: Chain Delegation for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens

abstract.t: This specification defines the delegation_chain JWT claim for OAuth 2.0 access tokens, enabling secure multi-hop delegation in agent-to-agent scenarios. It provides a cryptographically verifiable chain of delegation events, ensuring end-to-end auditability and preventing privilege escalation across delegation hops. The specification supports cross-domain delegation by composing with the identity and authorization chaining transport pattern, and integrates a user interaction mechanism that allows the authorization server to request explicit user consent during the delegation flow when required by policy or regulation.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: In multi-agent systems, a primary agent (Agent A) may need to delegate a subset of its authorized operations to a secondary agent (Agent B). While RFC 8693 Token Exchange provides mechanisms for delegation, it does not define how to maintain a verifiable chain of delegation events across multiple hops.
This specification introduces the delegation_chain claim, which:

ul.li: Records each delegation hop with cryptographic signatures;
Preserves end-to-end auditability back to the original human principal;
Prevents privilege escalation beyond the original authorization scope;
Enables Resource Servers to validate the complete delegation lineage.

section.t: This specification complements the act claim defined in by providing detailed delegation history, while act identifies the immediate actor.

This work directly addresses the "Complex Delegation" work item identified in the OAuth Working Group charter, which calls for developing new mechanisms and extensions for authorization of automated agents working on behalf of users, including addressing scenarios where automated agents act across multiple administrative domains. The delegation_chain claim provides the verifiable audit trail required for such complex delegation scenarios, while this specification's cross-domain delegation support () enables delegation across administrative boundaries.

This specification is designed as a layer that complements the cross-domain identity and authorization chaining mechanism defined in . That specification defines the transport pattern for crossing trust domain boundaries using Token Exchange and JWT Bearer grants. This specification defines the delegation audit data model — the delegation_chain claim — which can be used independently within a single trust domain or in combination with identity chaining for cross-domain delegation. The layered relationship is: identity chaining provides the "how to cross domains" infrastructure, while this specification provides the "how to prove delegation lineage" audit structure.
Conformance Profiles: This specification supports two conformance profiles to accommodate different deployment scenarios:

ul.li: Core Profile: Implementations need only support the delegation_chain claim structure (), the delegation Token Exchange flow (), and the AS validation rules (). The Core Profile does not require cross-domain support, user interaction (JAG-IR), Rego policy, or authorization evidence. It is suitable for single-domain deployments that need multi-hop delegation audit trails with standard OAuth scope constraints.

Full Profile: Implementations additionally support cross-domain delegation (), user interaction during delegation (), machine-enforceable policy via Rego (), and cryptographic authorization evidence (). The Full Profile is intended for multi-domain, regulated environments where fine-grained policy enforcement and auditable user consent are required.

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

dl.dd: An agent that transfers a subset of its authorization to another agent.
An agent that receives delegated authorization from a delegator.
A single transfer of authorization from one agent to another.
An ordered sequence of delegation hops from the most recent back to the original authorization.
The original authorization granted by a human principal, from which all delegations derive.

A token that cryptographically attests to the identity of a workload or agent, typically issued by a workload identity provider. A WIT URI is a URI that identifies a specific agent and references the WIT bound to that agent's identity.

section.title: Structure
section.t: The delegation_chain is an ordered array of delegation records, from most recent to earliest. Each record represents one delegation hop.

section.title: Delegation Lifecycle
section.t: A delegation record transitions through four phases during its lifecycle:

ol.li: Delegation Proposal Phase: The delegating agent creates a delegation proposal that includes the delegated policy, delegatee identity, and operation context. This phase corresponds to the policy creation process defined in .

Delegation Interaction Phase (CONDITIONAL): When the Authorization Server determines that user interaction is required before the delegation can be authorized — for example, when delegating to a new agent for the first time, when the delegation involves high-risk operations, or when the delegation crosses trust domain boundaries — the AS returns an interaction_required response as defined in . The delegating agent launches the interaction URI so the user can review and approve the delegation. Upon user approval, the agent retries the delegation request. This phase is skipped when the AS determines that no additional user interaction is needed (e.g., the delegation is covered by a standing authorization or the policy has been pre-approved).

Delegation Enforcement Phase: The Authorization Server validates the delegation request, verifies user identity (using JWT assertion via ID-JAG as defined in for the first delegation), confirms that any required user interaction has been completed, and signs the delegation record upon successful validation.
Chain Propagation Phase: The signed delegation record is embedded into an access token's delegation_chain claim, enabling multi-hop propagation across trust domains.

section.t: This four-phase model ensures cryptographic binding between user authorization, agent identity, and policy constraints throughout the delegation chain, with explicit user interaction support when required.

section.title: Field Definitions

tr.td: A URI identifying the delegating agent. Implementations SHOULD use a WIT URI when workload identity attestation is available. Alternatively, implementations MAY use other URI schemes (e.g., did:, https:, or a SPIFFE ID spiffe://) to identify the delegating agent, provided the URI is resolvable to a verifiable public key for delegator_signature verification.
A URI identifying the receiving agent. The same identifier format considerations as delegator_wit apply.

A subset of the delegator's authorized policy that is being delegated to the delegatee. This field SHOULD follow the structure defined in . The delegated policy MUST be equal to or more restrictive than the delegator's policy. Policy permission expansion is NOT allowed. When this field is absent, the delegation is governed solely by the OAuth scope parameter, and the Resource Server MUST apply scope-based authorization only. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to always include this field to enable fine-grained policy enforcement at the Resource Server.

Reference to the root authorization evidence record as defined in . This field MUST be present for the first delegation (User → Agent A) and SHOULD be propagated through the chain. The value SHOULD match the evidence.id from the root token.

Cryptographic signature from the delegating agent's private key over this delegation record. This provides dual-signature security alongside as_signature, preventing malicious AS from forging unauthorized delegations and ensuring non-repudiation.
AS signature over this delegation record.

section.t: The delegation_timestamp MUST satisfy the following constraints:

ul.li: It MUST be greater than or equal to the delegation_timestamp of the preceding delegation record (the record at the next higher array index), ensuring that timestamps are monotonically non-increasing from index 0 (most recent) to index N (earliest);

It MUST be within the validity period of the delegator's token at the time of the delegation request (i.e., greater than or equal to the delegator token's iat and less than or equal to the delegator token's exp).

section.t: The as_signature, and the delegator_signature when present, MUST be computed over the same set of fields using JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) as defined in :

ul.li: delegated_policy (if present)
operation_summary (if present)
root_evidence_ref (if present)

section.t: Both signature fields MUST be excluded from their respective signature computations. The signatures MUST use detached JWS format ( Appendix F) with appropriate algorithm identifiers (e.g., RS256, ES256).
The delegator_signature uses the delegating agent's WIT-bound private key, while as_signature uses the Authorization Server's signing key. This dual-signature approach ensures:

ul.li: Malicious AS Prevention: A compromised AS cannot unilaterally forge delegations without the delegator's consent;
Non-Repudiation: The delegator cannot deny having authorized the delegation;
Complete Trust Chain: User → AS → Delegator → Delegatee.

section.title: Chain Ordering
section.t: The array MUST be ordered from most recent delegation to earliest:

ul.li: Index 0: Most recent delegation (delegator → current token holder)
Index N: Earliest delegation (first agent after human authorization)

section.t: This ordering allows efficient validation starting from the immediate delegator.

section.title: Delegation with User Interaction
section.t: This section defines the primary delegation flow for chain delegation, which includes explicit user interaction to ensure user consent and awareness when agents delegate authorization. This flow extends the JWT Authorization Grant Interaction Response () to OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange requests (, grant_type=token-exchange).

The user interaction mechanism is a core feature of chain delegation, ensuring that delegation decisions remain under user control even in complex multi-agent scenarios. When the Authorization Server determines that user interaction is required, the flow includes an explicit consent step before token issuance.

section.title: Step 1-2: Initial Authorization
section.t: Agent A obtains authorization from the user through a standard OAuth flow. The resulting token does not contain a delegation_chain (it is the root authorization).

section.title: Step 3: Delegation Request
section.t: Agent A initiates delegation using OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange . The request includes delegation-specific parameters to identify the delegatee and the delegated policy.

figure.artwork:
POST /token HTTP/1.1 Host: as.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded OAuth-Client-Attestation: eyJ0eXAiOiJ3aXQrand0IiwiYWxnIjoiRVMyNTYifQ... OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJvYXV0aC1jbGllbnQtYXR0ZXN0...
grant_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Agrant-type%3Atoken-exchange &subject_token=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9... &subject_token_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Atoken-type%3Aaccess_token &requested_token_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Atoken-type%3Aaccess_token &scope=cart%3Aread &authorization_details=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22rego_policy%22%2C%22policy%22 %3A%7B%22type%22%3A%22rego%22%2C%22content%22%3A%22package+agent...%22%2C %22entry_point%22%3A%22allow%22%7D%7D%5D &delegatee_wit=wit%3A%2F%2Fagent-b.example%2Fsha256.bbb222...

section.t: This specification defines the following extension parameter for use with Token Exchange requests:

dl.dd: REQUIRED for delegation requests. A URI identifying the agent receiving the delegated authorization. Implementations SHOULD use a WIT URI when workload identity attestation is available, but MAY use other URI schemes (see ). The AS uses this value to bind the issued token to the delegatee's identity and to populate the delegatee_wit field in the delegation_chain record.

section.t: The standard and extension parameters in the request are:

ul.li: subject_token: Agent A's current access token;
subject_token_type: urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token;
delegatee_wit: The WIT URI of the delegatee agent (Agent B);
scope (OPTIONAL): Requested scope for the delegated token, which MUST be a subset of Agent A's scope.
requested_token_type (OPTIONAL): Defaults to urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token. Implementations MAY request JWT format using urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt.

resource (OPTIONAL): The identifier of the target Authorization Server when the delegation crosses a trust domain boundary, as defined in . When present, the AS issues a JWT authorization grant suitable for presentation to the target AS instead of a direct access token.

audience (OPTIONAL): A well-known or logical name of the target Authorization Server, as an alternative to resource for cross-domain delegation. One of resource or audience is REQUIRED when the delegation targets an agent in a different trust domain.

interaction_callback_uri (OPTIONAL): The URI to which the AS will redirect the user's browser after a delegation interaction is complete, as defined in . This parameter is used in conjunction with the interaction_required response to signal the client that user interaction has been completed.

section.title: Step 4: User Interaction Required
section.t: The Authorization Server SHOULD require user interaction before authorizing a delegation in the following scenarios:

ul.li: The delegation targets a new agent not covered by a standing authorization;
The delegation involves high-risk or high-value operations;
The delegation crosses trust domain boundaries;
Regulatory requirements mandate explicit, auditable user consent.

section.t: When user interaction is required, the AS responds with an interaction_required error containing:

ul.li: interaction_uri: The URI where the user reviews and approves the delegation;
interval: The minimum polling interval in seconds (default: 5);
expires_in: The number of seconds until the interaction session expires.

section.t: defines the interaction response mechanism for the JWT Authorization Grant (RFC 7523, grant_type=jwt-bearer). This specification extends that interaction response to apply to OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange requests (, grant_type=token-exchange) used for delegation. The same response semantics are applicable to Token Exchange requests. The AS associates the interaction session with the Token Exchange request parameters (including the subject_token, delegatee_wit, and requested delegation policy) so that upon user approval, the same Token Exchange request can be retried to obtain the delegated token.

section.title: Steps 5-7: User Review and Approval
section.t: Agent A launches the interaction_uri in the user's browser, where the AS presents the delegation details for user review:

ul.li: Identity of the delegatee agent (Agent B)
Delegated policy and scope
Operation summary
Whether the delegation crosses trust domain boundaries

section.t: The user reviews the delegation details and approves or denies the delegation request. If the client provided an interaction_callback_uri, the AS redirects the user's browser to that URI as a signal that the interaction is complete.

section.title: Step 8: Retry Token Exchange
section.t: Agent A retries the original Token Exchange request (with the same parameters). The AS recognizes the associated interaction session and proceeds with validation.

While the interaction is pending, subsequent Token Exchange requests from Agent A with the same parameters SHOULD return an interaction_pending error. The agent MUST wait at least the number of seconds specified by the interval parameter between polling requests.

section.title: Step 9: AS Validation
section.t: The AS MUST perform the following validations:

ol.li: Interaction Completion: Verify that user interaction has been completed and approved for this delegation request.
Token Validity: Verify Agent A's token is valid and not revoked.
Delegation Permission: Confirm the token permits delegation (e.g., includes a delegation scope or flag).
Scope Subset: Verify the requested scope is a subset of Agent A's authorized scope (equal to or narrower).
Delegatee Authentication: Validate Agent B's workload identity token (WIT).
Chain Depth: Optionally enforce maximum delegation depth.

section.title: Step 10: Token Issuance
section.t: Upon successful validation, the AS issues a new token for Agent B with:

ul.li: sub: The original user (unchanged)
act: Agent B's identity
delegation_chain: Extended with a new record for this hop
Reduced scope (as requested)

section.title: Steps 11-12: API Request and Validation
section.t: Agent B uses the delegated token to access resources at the Resource Server (RS). The RS validates the token and verifies the delegation_chain as defined in .

section.title: Simplified Delegation via Token Exchange
section.t: In scenarios where user interaction is not required — for example, when the delegation is covered by a standing authorization or the policy has been pre-approved — the AS MAY skip the user interaction step and proceed directly with token issuance. This simplified flow reduces latency and user friction for routine delegation scenarios.
When none of the conditions listed in apply, the AS responds to the Token Exchange request with a success response containing the delegated token, bypassing the interaction_required step.

The Token Exchange request format, parameters, and validation rules are identical to those defined in . The only difference is that the AS does not require user interaction before issuing the delegated token.
This simplified flow is appropriate when:

ul.li: The delegation is covered by a standing authorization previously granted by the user;
The delegated policy is equal to or more restrictive than a previously user-approved policy;
The delegation does not cross trust domain boundaries;
The delegation does not involve high-risk operations;
No regulatory requirements mandate explicit user consent.

section.t: Authorization Servers SHOULD log all decisions to skip user interaction as part of the audit trail defined in .

section.title: Chain Extension
section.t: When the AS issues a delegated token, it extends the delegation_chain:

section.title: Evidence Propagation
section.t: When the AS issues a delegated token within the same trust domain, it MUST propagate the evidence and audit_trail claims from the subject token (or root token) into the newly issued delegated token. This ensures that Resource Servers can verify the original user consent without needing to retrieve the root token separately. The root_evidence_ref field in each delegation record MUST match the evidence.id value in the propagated evidence claim. For cross-domain evidence propagation, see .

section.title: Cross-Domain Delegation
section.t: When delegation hops span multiple trust domains — each with its own Authorization Server — this specification combines the delegation_chain audit model with the cross-domain transport pattern defined in .

section.title: Cross-Domain Delegation Flow
section.t: Consider an agent in Trust Domain A that needs to delegate a subset of its authorization to an agent in Trust Domain B:

ol.li: Agent A obtains initial authorization from the user in Trust Domain A (root authorization, no delegation_chain).

Agent A initiates a delegation Token Exchange with AS-A, including the resource parameter set to AS-B's identifier (as defined in ). This signals that the delegation targets an agent in Trust Domain B.

AS-A validates the delegation, creates a delegation record, and returns a JWT authorization grant containing the delegation_chain claim. If user interaction is required, the interaction flow described in is used before this step.
Agent A presents the JWT authorization grant to AS-B using the JWT Bearer grant type (), as defined in .
AS-B validates the JWT grant signature, verifies the delegation_chain (including AS-A's signature on each record), and confirms policy narrowing constraints.
AS-B issues an access token to Agent B for Trust Domain B, preserving the delegation_chain claim from the JWT authorization grant.
Agent B uses the access token to access resources in Trust Domain B.

section.title: Cross-Domain Trust Requirements
section.t: For cross-domain delegation to function, the following trust requirements MUST be satisfied:

ul.li: AS Trust Relationship: AS-B MUST trust AS-A's signing key to verify as_signature on delegation records issued by AS-A. This trust relationship is typically established through key exchange or by publishing AS-A's public keys via Authorization Server Metadata ().

delegation_chain Propagation: AS-B MUST propagate the delegation_chain claim from the JWT authorization grant into the access token it issues, so that Resource Servers in Trust Domain B can validate the full delegation lineage.

Evidence Propagation: AS-B SHOULD propagate the evidence and audit_trail claims from the JWT authorization grant, enabling Resource Servers in Trust Domain B to verify the original user consent without contacting AS-A. This is a SHOULD rather than a MUST because cross-domain evidence propagation may be constrained by data minimization policies, privacy regulations, or trust agreements between domains. When evidence is not propagated, Resource Servers in Trust Domain B MUST rely on back-channel verification with AS-A or AS-B to validate the original user consent.

Policy Enforcement: AS-B MUST enforce that the delegated policy in the delegation_chain is equal to or more restrictive than the policy in the JWT authorization grant. Policy expansion across domain boundaries is NOT permitted.

section.title: Multi-Domain Chain Extension
section.t: When a delegation chain spans multiple domains, each domain's AS may add delegation records to the chain. The cross-domain transport uses the identity chaining pattern (Token Exchange + JWT Bearer Grant) at each domain boundary, while the delegation_chain accumulates records from all domains.
Resource Servers validating a cross-domain delegation chain MUST:

ul.li: Verify trust relationships between all ASes referenced in the chain;
Verify chain continuity and policy narrowing across domain boundaries.

section.title: Relationship to Related Specifications
section.t: This specification is part of a family of specifications that together address the Complex Delegation problem for automated agents. This section describes how these specifications relate to each other and how they compose into a complete solution.

section.title: Specification Ecosystem
section.t: The following diagram illustrates how the related specifications compose into a layered solution for complex agent delegation:

figure.artwork: +---------------------------------------------------------------+ | Complex Delegation Ecosystem | +---------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | +-------------------+ +--------------------+ | | | Authorization | | Rego Policy | | | | Evidence | | Language | | | | [authz-evidence] | | [rego-policy] | | | | | | | | | | Records user | | Defines machine- | | | | consent with | | enforceable policy | | | | cryptographic | | constraints for | | | | proof | | each delegation | | | +--------+----------+ +--------+-----------+ | | | | | | v v | | +--------+------------------------+-----------+ | | | Chain Delegation [this spec] | | | | | | | | delegation_chain claim with dual-signature | | | | audit trail across all delegation hops | | | +--------+------------------------+-----------+ | | | ^ | | v | | | +--------+----------+ +--------+-----------+ | | | JAG-IR | | Identity Chaining | | | | [jwt-grant-ir] | | [identity-chain] | | | | | | | | | | User interaction | | Cross-domain token | | | | when delegation | | transport via | | | | requires consent | | Token Exchange + | | | | | | JWT Bearer Grant | | | +--------------------+ +--------------------+ | | | +---------------------------------------------------------------+

section.t: Each specification addresses a distinct concern:

ul.li: Authorization Evidence (): Records the original user consent with cryptographic proof, providing the trust anchor for all downstream delegations;
Rego Policy Language (): Defines machine-enforceable policy constraints that govern what operations each agent is authorized to perform;
Chain Delegation (this specification): Defines the delegation_chain claim — the auditable, cryptographically signed record of each delegation hop, with policy narrowing enforcement;
JAG-IR (): Provides the user interaction mechanism for delegation flows that require explicit user consent mid-flow;
Identity Chaining (): Provides the cross-domain transport mechanism for crossing trust domain boundaries during delegation.

section.title: Relationship to OAuth Identity Chaining
section.t: This specification profiles and extends the identity and authorization chaining mechanism defined in . That specification defines a general-purpose pattern combining Token Exchange () and JWT Bearer grants for cross-domain identity propagation. This specification reuses that Token Exchange pattern for the delegation request () and adds the following agent-specific extensions:

ul.li: Policy narrowing enforcement: Each delegation hop MUST carry a policy equal to or more restrictive than its predecessor, enforced via Rego policy in authorization_details;
WIT-based agent identity: Attestation-based workload identity (WIT) vs. pre-configured PKI trust.

section.t: The key distinctions in deployment context are:

ul.li: Scope Control: Mandatory policy contraction vs. static claims transcription;
Time Scale: Task-level (minutes/hours) vs. employment-level (months/years);
Target: AI agent workloads vs. human users and services.

section.t: Implementations MAY use WIT with attestation evidence for enhanced security, but it is not required by this specification.

section.title: Relationship to JAG-IR
section.t: The JWT Authorization Grant Interaction Response () defines a mechanism for an Authorization Server to indicate that user interaction is required before completing a JWT Authorization Grant request. This specification uses JAG-IR as the interaction mechanism during the Delegation Interaction Phase ():

ul.li: After user approval, the agent retries the delegation Token Exchange request, and the AS proceeds with token issuance.

section.t: The combination of chain delegation and JAG-IR ensures that every delegation hop in a multi-agent chain can be individually authorized by the user when policy or regulation requires it, without disrupting the overall delegation flow.

section.title: Resource Server Validation
section.t: Resource Servers validate the delegation_chain as follows:

section.title: Signature Verification
section.t: For each record in the chain, verify the as_signature using the AS's public key. This ensures:

ul.li: The delegation was authorized by the AS;
The record has not been tampered with;
The delegation metadata is authentic.

section.title: Root Authorization Anchor
section.t: The last record in the chain (highest index) represents the earliest delegation. Its delegator_wit identifies the agent that holds the root authorization (the token directly authorized by the user).
The Resource Server MUST verify that:

ul.li: The earliest delegator (last record) holds a root token — a token without a delegation_chain claim;
This root token was issued by a trusted AS and has not been revoked.
The root token contains valid evidence and audit_trail claims as defined in , providing cryptographic proof of user consent.

section.t: If the RS cannot verify the root authorization anchor, it MUST reject the request.

section.title: Dual-Signature Verification
section.t: For each delegation record, the Resource Server SHOULD verify both:

ul.li: AS Signature: Using the Authorization Server's public key, confirming the delegation was authorized by the AS;
Delegator Signature: Using the delegating agent's WIT-bound public key, confirming the delegator explicitly consented to this delegation.

section.t: The dual-signature mechanism prevents:

ul.li: Malicious AS from unilaterally forging delegations;
Delegators from denying authorized delegations (non-repudiation);
Unauthorized privilege escalation through compromised components.

section.title: WIT Status Validation
section.t: The Resource Server SHOULD verify the current status of all Workload Identity Tokens (WITs) referenced in the delegation_chain by:

ul.li: Checking WIT revocation lists or status endpoints;
Validating WIT expiration timestamps;
Querying the issuing Identity Provider for current status.

section.t: If any WIT in the chain has been revoked or expired, the entire delegation_chain MUST be considered invalid, even if individual records remain cryptographically valid.

section.title: Chain Continuity
section.t: Verify the chain is continuous:

ul.li: For each record at index i (where i > 0), record[i].delegator_wit MUST equal record[i-1].delegatee_wit, ensuring that the agent who received authorization in one hop is the same agent that delegates in the next hop;
The delegatee_wit of the most recent delegation record (index 0) matches the token's act.sub;
Timestamps are in descending order.

section.title: Scope Validation
section.t: Verify scope constraints are progressively narrowing:

ul.li: Each delegation's delegated_policy MUST be equal to or more restrictive than the previous delegation's policy
The final scope MUST cover the requested operation.

section.title: Threat Model
section.t: This section describes the threat model underlying the delegation_chain mechanism and the security properties it provides.

ul.li: The Authorization Server (AS) is trusted to correctly validate delegation requests, enforce policy narrowing, and sign delegation records with its private key. The AS is the central trust anchor for the delegation chain.
The human principal (end user) is trusted to make informed authorization decisions during consent and interaction flows.
A malicious delegatee agent may attempt to present a token with a forged or truncated delegation_chain to claim authorization it does not possess.
A malicious delegator agent may attempt to delegate more authorization than it was granted (privilege escalation), or may deny having authorized a delegation (repudiation).
A compromised AS may attempt to forge delegation records without the delegator's consent. The dual-signature mechanism (delegator + AS) mitigates this threat.
A network attacker may attempt to intercept or modify delegation records in transit. Standard TLS protections apply to all protocol messages.

section.t: Security Objectives: The delegation_chain claim provides the following security properties:

ul.li: Integrity: Each delegation record is cryptographically signed by the AS (and optionally the delegator), preventing undetected modification.
Non-repudiation: The delegator's signature on each record provides evidence that the delegation was explicitly authorized.
Policy compliance: Mandatory policy narrowing at each hop prevents privilege escalation through the chain.
Auditability: The complete chain from the current actor back to the original human principal enables end-to-end audit trail reconstruction.

section.title: Privilege Escalation Prevention
section.t: The AS MUST ensure that delegation cannot expand privileges:

ul.li: Delegated scope MUST be a subset of (equal to or narrower than) delegator's scope;
Delegation depth MAY be limited;
Certain scopes MAY be marked non-delegatable.

section.title: Chain Integrity
section.t: The as_signature on each record ensures chain integrity. Agents MUST NOT be able to:

ul.li: Forge delegation records;
Modify existing records;
Remove records from the chain;
Reorder records.

section.title: Chain Stripping Prevention
section.t: A malicious agent may attempt to present a token with a truncated or empty delegation_chain to hide intermediate delegation hops. For example, an agent holding a token with chain [A→B→C] could attempt to present only [A→C] or an empty chain.
This attack is prevented by the following mechanisms:

ul.li: Token-level signature: The AS signs the entire access token (including the delegation_chain claim) using its private key. Any modification to the delegation_chain claim — including removal of records or replacement with a shorter chain — invalidates the token's signature. The Resource Server MUST reject tokens whose signature does not verify.

Record-level signatures: Each delegation record carries an independent as_signature. Even if an attacker could reconstruct a token with a modified chain, the individual record signatures would not match a newly constructed chain without the AS's private key.

Token binding via act claim: The token's act claim identifies the current actor (the delegatee of the most recent hop). The Resource Server MUST verify that the delegatee_wit of the most recent delegation record (index 0) matches the token's act.sub. A stripped chain would fail this continuity check.

section.t: For opaque (non-JWT) access tokens, the Resource Server MUST use token introspection () to retrieve the authoritative delegation_chain from the AS, rather than trusting any client-supplied chain data.

section.title: Token Binding
section.t: Each delegation record is cryptographically bound to specific agent identities via WIT URIs and AS signatures. This enables:

ul.li: Revocation of specific delegation paths;
Audit trail reconstruction;
Detection of token reuse.

section.title: Delegation Depth Limits
section.t: Implementations SHOULD enforce maximum delegation depth to:

ul.li: Prevent unbounded delegation chains;
Limit token size growth;
Simplify validation.

section.t: A RECOMMENDED default maximum depth is 5 hops.

Implementers should consider the impact of delegation chain depth on token size. Each delegation record typically adds 500 to 1000 bytes to the token payload, including two detached JWS signatures (approximately 200 bytes each for ES256) and the Rego policy content. A 5-hop delegation chain may therefore add 2.5 to 5 KB to the access token. This can cause issues with:

ul.li: HTTP header size limits (commonly 8 KB in default proxy configurations);
TLS record size constraints;
Client and server memory consumption during token parsing.

section.t: To mitigate token size growth, implementations MAY use short-lived tokens with token introspection () to retrieve the delegation_chain on demand, or MAY compress policy content when the policy language supports it.

section.title: Cross-Domain Trust
section.t: When delegation chains span multiple trust domains, additional security considerations apply:

ul.li: AS Key Trust: Resource Servers in each trust domain must be able to verify as_signature on delegation records issued by Authorization Servers in other trust domains. This requires establishing cross-domain key trust relationships, which may be achieved through key exchange agreements, published JWKS endpoints (), or a shared trust framework. Failure to properly verify cross-domain AS signatures may allow forged delegation records to be accepted.

Claim Semantics Across Domains: Claims such as sub, scope, and policy identifiers may have different semantics across trust domains. Implementations MUST ensure that claim interpretation is consistent or explicitly mapped at each domain boundary, following the claims transcription guidance in .

Revocation Propagation: When the root authorization or any intermediate delegation is revoked, all downstream delegated tokens SHOULD be invalidated. Within a single trust domain, the AS can directly revoke delegated tokens. Across trust domains, implementations SHOULD mitigate the risk of stale delegated tokens through one or more of the following approaches: issuing short-lived delegated tokens to minimize the revocation window, implementing back-channel revocation notifications between ASes (e.g., using Token Revocation or a proprietary notification mechanism), or requiring Resource Servers in the downstream domain to perform token introspection () before accepting delegated tokens.

Lateral Movement: An attacker who compromises an agent in one trust domain may attempt to use the delegation chain to move laterally to other trust domains. Cross-domain delegation SHOULD be restricted by policy to only the trust domains explicitly authorized by the original user consent.

section.title: When to Require Interaction
section.t: The Authorization Server has discretion in determining when the Delegation Interaction Phase is triggered. The following guidance is provided to help AS implementations make consistent decisions:

ul.li: First-time delegation to a new agent: When the delegatee agent has not been previously authorized by the user, interaction SHOULD be required to ensure the user is aware of and consents to the new delegation relationship.

High-risk operations: When the delegated policy includes operations classified as high-risk (e.g., financial transactions, data deletion, access to sensitive resources), interaction SHOULD be required regardless of whether the agent has been previously authorized.

Cross-domain delegation: When a delegation hop crosses a trust domain boundary, interaction SHOULD be required unless a pre-established cross-domain trust agreement covers the specific delegation pattern.

Standing authorization: When the user has previously granted a standing authorization that explicitly covers the delegation pattern (e.g., "Agent A may delegate inventory operations to any agent in the inventory.example.com domain"), interaction MAY be skipped.
Policy pre-approval: When the delegated policy is equal to or more restrictive than a previously user-approved policy for the same delegatee, interaction MAY be skipped.

section.t: Authorization Servers SHOULD log all interaction decisions (whether interaction was required or skipped) as part of the audit trail defined in .

section.title: Delegation Revocation
section.t: Revocation of delegated authorization is a critical security operation. This section defines the revocation semantics for delegation chains.

ul.li: Root revocation: When the original user revokes the root authorization (the token without a delegation_chain), all downstream delegated tokens derived from that root authorization MUST be considered invalid. Resource Servers validating a delegation chain MUST verify that the root authorization remains valid, either by checking the root token's status directly or by using token introspection () on the root token.

Intermediate hop revocation: When a delegating agent revokes a specific delegation hop (e.g., Agent A revokes its delegation to Agent B), all tokens derived from that delegation — including further downstream delegations (Agent B → Agent C → Agent D) — MUST be considered invalid. Resource Servers MUST verify that no delegation record in the chain has been revoked, which can be checked through the delegator's revocation status endpoint or by introspecting the subject token of each hop.

Delegatee token revocation: When a delegatee agent's own token is revoked, only that specific token is affected. The delegation chain record itself remains valid for audit purposes, but the delegatee can no longer use the delegated authorization.

section.t: Revocation Detection Mechanisms: Resource Servers and downstream Authorization Servers MUST implement at least one of the following mechanisms to detect delegation revocation:

ul.li: Short-lived tokens: Issue delegated tokens with short expiration times (e.g., 5 to 15 minutes) to limit the window during which a revoked delegation remains effective;
Token introspection: Perform token introspection () on each token in the delegation chain before accepting the delegated authorization, confirming that no token has been revoked;

Back-channel revocation notifications: Subscribe to revocation events from upstream Authorization Servers using Token Revocation () or a proprietary notification mechanism, enabling proactive invalidation of downstream delegated tokens.

section.t: Audit Trail Preservation: Even after a delegation hop is revoked, the delegation record MUST be preserved in the delegation_chain claim for audit trail reconstruction purposes. Revocation invalidates the authorization but does not erase the evidence that the delegation occurred.

section.title: Privacy Considerations
section.t: In addition to the privacy considerations outlined in and , the following privacy considerations apply to the delegation_chain mechanism defined in this specification.

section.title: Data Minimization
section.t: The delegation_chain claim carries identity and authorization information about the original user, all intermediate agents, and the delegation policies. As the chain grows with each hop, the amount of information embedded in the token increases. Implementations should apply data minimization principles:

ul.li: The operation_summary field is OPTIONAL and should contain only the minimum information necessary for authorization decisions, not detailed descriptions of user intent or behavior.
The delegated_policy should be scoped to the specific operations being delegated, not include broader context about the user's overall authorization.
Agent identifiers (delegator_wit, delegatee_wit) should be pseudonymous where possible, avoiding direct exposure of personally identifiable information.

section.title: Cross-Domain Information Leakage
section.t: When delegation chains cross trust domain boundaries, the delegation_chain claim propagates user and agent identity information from the originating domain to downstream domains. This creates the following privacy risks:

ul.li: The sub claim reveals the original user's identity in the originating domain to all downstream domains. Implementations should consider identifier mapping or pairwise pseudonymous identifiers, following the claims transcription guidance in .

The evidence claim may contain details about the user's consent interaction (e.g., displayed content, session context, channel). Downstream domains receive this information. ASes should minimize the evidence payload or apply domain-specific filtering before cross-domain propagation.
The complete delegation chain reveals the full topology of agent relationships, which may be sensitive in competitive or multi-tenant environments.

section.title: User Consent Transparency
section.t: When the Delegation Interaction Phase is triggered (as described in ), the user is presented with delegation details for review and approval. Implementations should ensure that the consent UI clearly communicates:

ul.li: The identity of the delegatee agent receiving the delegation;
The specific operations being delegated;
Whether the delegation crosses trust domain boundaries;
The user's ability to revoke the delegation at any time.

section.title: JWT Claims Registration
section.t: This specification registers the following claim in the "JSON Web Token Claims" registry:

dl.dd: An ordered array of AS-signed delegation records tracing agent-to-agent authorization transfers, enabling end-to-end validation of delegation lineage.

section.title: OAuth Parameters Registration
section.t: This specification registers the following parameters in the "OAuth Parameters" registry established by Section 11.2:

dl.dd: of this document. This parameter is used in the token request context to receive a redirect callback upon completion of user interaction, as extended from . This is a distinct parameter from the redirect_uri defined in Section 3.1.2, which is used in authorization requests.

section.title: OAuth Error Registration
section.t: This specification defines the following error codes for use in delegation Token Exchange responses. These errors extend the OAuth 2.0 error registry established by Section 11.4:

dl.dd: The delegation_chain claim in the presented token fails validation (e.g., broken chain continuity, invalid signatures, or expired timestamps). The AS MUST reject the delegation request.
The delegation chain has reached the maximum number of hops permitted by the AS policy, and the requested delegation would exceed this limit.
The requested delegated_policy or scope is broader than the delegator's authorized policy, violating the policy narrowing constraint defined in .

section.t: The following shows a token held by Agent C after two delegation hops (User → Agent A → Agent B → Agent C):
This token shows:

ul.li: Original user: user_12345
Current actor: Agent C
Delegation path: Agent A → Agent B → Agent C

Original user consent evidence preserved

section.title: Validation Mechanism
section.t: Each delegation hop MUST be represented as a separate JWT access token issued and signed by the Authorization Server. The delegating agent additionally provides a delegator_signature within the delegation_chain record for dual-signature non-repudiation.

section.title: Token Structure
section.t: For each delegation from Agent-X to Agent-Y, the AS issues a new access token where:

ul.li: The token's "iss" claim MUST be the Authorization Server's identifier
The token's "sub" claim MUST be the original user's identifier (preserved from root authorization)
The token's "act" claim MUST identify the delegatee agent (Agent-Y)
The token MUST be signed by the Authorization Server's private key
The token's "delegation_chain" claim accumulates all previous hops

section.title: Verification Requirements
section.t: Resource Servers MUST validate:

ol.li: The final token's signature matches the claimed issuer
Each hop in the delegation_chain has valid timestamps
Policy constraints are maintained or reduced (never expanded)
The chain is continuous: for each record at index i (where i > 0), record[i].delegator_wit equals record[i-1].delegatee_wit
The initial delegator matches the original authorization subject

section.title: Per-Hop Signing Security Properties
section.t: This per-hop signing approach provides:

ul.li: Non-repudiation: Each delegator's signature is independent evidence
Flexible revocation: Individual hops can be revoked separately
Incremental updates: New hops only require generating new tokens
Audit-friendly: Each signature represents a discrete authorization event

section.title: Implementation Guidance
section.t: [[ This section provides non-normative guidance for implementers. ]]

section.title: Opaque vs. JWT Access Tokens
section.t: The delegation_chain claim is defined for JWT-format access tokens. When implementations use opaque (reference) access tokens, the delegation chain is not embedded in the token itself. Instead, the Resource Server retrieves the complete delegation chain via token introspection (). Implementations using opaque tokens SHOULD ensure that the introspection response includes the delegation_chain claim, the evidence claim, and the act claim, enabling the Resource Server to perform full chain validation without requiring direct access to the token's JWT payload.

section.title: Token Size Mitigation
section.t: As noted in , each delegation record adds approximately 500 to 1000 bytes to the token payload. Implementations can mitigate token size growth through the following approaches:

ul.li: Short-lived tokens with introspection: Issue access tokens with short expiration (e.g., 5 minutes) and rely on token introspection to retrieve the delegation_chain on demand. This keeps the token compact while preserving full validation capability.

Policy references: Instead of embedding the full Rego policy in each delegation record, store policies in a shared policy store and reference them by identifier. The delegated_policy field then contains only a reference (e.g., a URI), reducing per-record size significantly. This approach requires Resource Servers to have access to the policy store.

Compression: Apply compression to the JWT payload when the token transport supports it (e.g., HTTP with Content-Encoding: gzip). Note that this is a transport-level optimization and does not reduce the logical token size.

section.title: Library Integration
section.t: Implementations integrating delegation_chain support into existing OAuth 2.0 libraries should consider:

ul.li: Token validation middleware: Extend existing JWT validation middleware to include delegation_chain verification (signature checks, chain continuity, policy narrowing) as a post-validation step. This allows the core token validation (issuer, expiration, audience) to remain unchanged.

Policy evaluation: When using Rego policies (), embed a lightweight policy evaluator (e.g., Open Policy Agent's Go library) into the Resource Server. For the Core Profile, standard scope-based authorization is sufficient and no policy engine is required.

Agent identity resolution: When delegator_wit or delegatee_wit uses alternative URI schemes (e.g., did:, spiffe://), integrate the appropriate resolver (DID resolver, SPIFFE bundle endpoint) to retrieve the public key for signature verification.

section.title: Performance Considerations
section.t: Resource Server validation of a delegation_chain involves multiple cryptographic operations. For a chain of N hops, the RS must verify:

ul.li: 1 token-level signature (the access token itself);
N AS signatures (one per delegation record);
Up to N delegator signatures (if delegator_signature is present on each record).

section.t: For a 5-hop chain, this results in up to 11 signature verifications. Using ECDSA (ES256) on modern hardware, each verification takes approximately 0.1 to 0.5 milliseconds, yielding a total validation latency of 1 to 5 milliseconds for the chain — well within typical API response time budgets. Implementations SHOULD cache AS public keys (via JWKS endpoints) and WIT-bound public keys to avoid repeated key lookups.
